front.title: Authorization Evidence and Audit Trail for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens

abstract.t: This specification defines an authorization details type for including authorization evidence and audit trail information in OAuth 2.0 access tokens using the Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) framework. When an Authorization Server processes user consent, it enriches the authorization details with cryptographic proof of user confirmation, supporting accountability, compliance, and dispute resolution in scenarios where autonomous agents act on behalf of users.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In traditional OAuth 2.0 flows, the Authorization Server records user consent internally, but this information is not typically conveyed to Resource Servers or included in access tokens. For many use cases, this is sufficient. However, emerging scenarios, particularly those involving AI agents acting autonomously on behalf of users, require stronger guarantees about user intent and consent.
This specification addresses the need for:

ul.li: Verifiable consent: Cryptographic proof that a user explicitly authorized a specific operation;
Audit trails: Traceable records linking user intent to system actions;
Dispute resolution: Evidence that can be examined if questions arise about what was authorized;

Consent withdrawal: A standardized, user-initiated mechanism to revoke previously granted consent. Withdrawal of consent is a first-class operation in autonomous agent scenarios, where consent is given asynchronously and may need to be withdrawn long after it was granted. Regulations in some jurisdictions further require that withdrawing consent be as easy as granting it;
Regulatory compliance: Documentation required by applicable regulations.

section.t: This specification defines an authorization details type that leverages the Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) framework to convey authorization evidence. When a client includes an authorization_evidence authorization details object in its request, the Authorization Server enriches it during the consent process with cryptographic proof of user confirmation. This specification also defines a consent revocation mechanism () that allows the user to withdraw previously granted consent, completing the consent lifecycle from grant through revocation.
Unless otherwise noted, all data types and serialization rules follow the JSON data interchange format as defined in .

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

section.title: Relationship to Rich Authorization Requests
section.t: This specification builds on the Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) framework . In RAR, clients include authorization_details in authorization requests to convey fine-grained authorization data. RAR Section 7.1 defines an "Enriched Response" mechanism where the Authorization Server dynamically populates fields in the authorization_details based on user consent decisions or policy rules.
The authorization_evidence type defined in this specification follows this enriched response pattern:

ol.li: The client includes an authorization_evidence authorization details object in its request, typically with minimal or placeholder fields indicating that evidence is requested.
During the consent interaction, the AS presents the requested operation to the user and captures the user's confirmation action.
The AS enriches the authorization_evidence object with the complete evidence record, including user_confirmation details and the AS's cryptographic signature.
The enriched authorization details is included in the token response and bound to the issued access token.

section.t: This approach ensures that authorization evidence is structured as a first-class authorization detail rather than a standalone JWT claim, enabling consistent handling across OAuth flows and composability with other authorization details types.

dl.dd: An explicit action by the user (e.g., clicking "Allow") to approve an authorization request.
The human-readable description of the operation shown to the user during the consent flow.
A cryptographically signed record of user confirmation, including what was displayed and how the user responded.
Metadata that enables tracing from user intent through system interpretation to final authorized action.
The process of translating user intent (e.g., natural language) into concrete system operations.

An Authorization Server-side entity created at the moment of consent, capturing the consent event and its lifecycle state. The consent record exists independently of any access token and is the anchor for revocation (see ).
A URI under the Authorization Server's control through which the user can initiate revocation of a specific consent record. The handle is a lookup key, not a credential.

section.title: The authorization_evidence Authorization Details Type
section.t: The authorization_evidence authorization details type contains a record of the user's confirmation action during the authorization process. Following the RAR enriched response pattern ( Section 7.1), the client requests this type and the AS enriches it with the complete evidence record.

dl.dd: authorization_evidence
authorization_details in authorization requests and token responses

section.title: Client Request
section.t: A client requests authorization evidence by including an authorization_evidence authorization details object in its authorization request. The client typically includes minimal fields, indicating that evidence is requested:

The client MAY include optional fields to indicate preferences, such as specific audit trail requirements. However, the AS has final authority over the evidence content based on the actual consent interaction.

section.title: Enriched Response
section.t: After the user completes the consent interaction, the AS enriches the authorization_evidence object with the complete evidence record. The enriched authorization details is included in the token response:

section.title: Evidence Object Structure
section.t: The evidence object within the authorization_evidence authorization details type contains the following fields:

tr.td: Unique identifier for this evidence record. The value MUST use a URI or URN format with at least 128 bits of collision resistance. UUID URNs (e.g., "urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6") are RECOMMENDED.
Details of the user's confirmation action.
AS signature over the confirmation record.
Revocation information for the consent recorded by this evidence, as defined in . This member is not covered by the as_signature (see ).
The text shown to user for confirmation.

How the user confirmed the operation. The value is a free-form string, but implementations SHOULD use values from the following set for interoperability: button_click, biometric_confirmation, pin_entry, voice_confirmation, hardware_key, implicit_consent. Custom values MAY be used for deployment-specific confirmation mechanisms.

section.title: AS Signature
section.t: The as_signature field contains a cryptographic signature from the Authorization Server over the evidence record. This signature:

ul.li: Proves the AS witnessed the user's consent;
Ensures the evidence has not been tampered with;
Provides strong evidence of user consent for dispute resolution (subject to trust in the AS, as discussed in ).

section.t: The signature MUST be computed over the following fields of the evidence object:

ul.li: user_confirmation (entire object)

section.t: The as_signature field itself MUST be excluded from the signature computation. The signature format MUST be a detached JWS in Compact Serialization using the AS's signing key. In detached Compact Serialization (see RFC 7515 Appendix F), the payload portion is omitted, resulting in the format "header..signature".
The signature input is constructed using the following deterministic algorithm:

ol.li: Create a new JSON object containing only the id and user_confirmation fields copied from the evidence object. No other fields from the evidence object are included.
Apply the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined in to the JSON object from the previous step, producing a deterministic byte string.

Compute a detached JWS (Compact Serialization) over the JCS output from Step 2 using the AS's private signing key. The resulting value (header..signature) is stored in the as_signature field of the evidence object.

section.t: To verify an as_signature, the verifier reconstructs the JCS input by performing Steps 1 and 2 above on the received evidence object (excluding the as_signature field), then verifies the detached JWS using the AS's public key. Any extension fields present in the evidence object beyond id, user_confirmation, and as_signature MUST NOT be included in the JCS input and therefore are not covered by the signature. In particular, the OPTIONAL revocation member defined in is not covered by the as_signature; in signed JWT access tokens its integrity is provided by the token signature.
Note: In examples throughout this document, the as_signature value is shown in abbreviated form for readability. Actual values MUST use the detached JWS Compact Serialization format described above.

The key used to sign the evidence record MAY be the same key used to sign the access token, or it MAY be a separate dedicated key. When a separate key is used, implementations MUST ensure that the evidence signing key is associated with the AS through a verifiable mechanism (e.g., published in the AS's JWKS endpoint as defined in ). Using a dedicated evidence signing key enables independent key rotation without affecting token validation.

section.title: The audit_trail Sub-object
section.t: The audit_trail sub-object provides metadata for semantic traceability, enabling analysis of how user intent was interpreted and translated into authorized operations. It is included within the evidence object in the authorization_evidence authorization details type.

tr.td: Reference to a related evidence record by ID. Can be used to link this audit trail to another evidence record, such as the original consent in a delegation chain.
Degree of interpretation applied (none, low, medium, high).

Reference to the original authorization proposal, the agent's initial request describing the intended operation before the AS applied policy evaluation, scope reduction, or user consent modifications. The value is an opaque URI assigned by the AS for internal correlation; no protocol for retrieving the proposal content via this URI is defined by this specification. This enables post-hoc comparison between what the agent originally requested and what was ultimately authorized.

section.title: Semantic Expansion Levels
section.t: The semantic_expansion_level field indicates how much the system interpreted or expanded the user's original intent. The following four values form a closed set; implementations MUST NOT use values outside this set:

dl.dd: No interpretation; user specified exact parameters. Example: User explicitly sets "transfer $100 to account X".
Minor defaults applied. Example: User says "add to cart" and the system defaults quantity to 1 and selects the user's saved shipping address.
Significant interpretation of qualitative terms. Example: User says "buy cheap headphones" and the system maps "cheap" to a price ceiling of $50 and selects a specific product category.

Substantial expansion from a high-level goal into a multi-step plan. Example: User says "plan my trip to Tokyo" and the agent derives flight search, hotel booking, and itinerary creation as separate authorized operations.

section.title: Audit Trail Purposes
section.t: The evidence and audit trail objects serve several important purposes:

tr.td: Records what the user intended, preventing disputes about authorization scope.
Documents how the system translated intent into operations, showing the reasoning process.
Reveals any expansions or defaults applied, enabling users to understand what was authorized.
Provides timestamped proof that the user reviewed and approved the operation.
Enables post-hoc analysis to determine responsibility for erroneous transactions.
Provides the revocation handle and status entry points () that allow the user to withdraw previously granted consent and allow auditors to resolve the current state of a consent.

section.title: Evidence Collection from User Interaction
section.t: The evidence object records the outcome of a user consent interaction. Before the AS can generate a signed evidence record, it must first present a consent interface to the user and capture the user's response. This section describes the general consent-to-evidence pattern and provides a concrete example using the JWT Grant Interaction Response flow.

section.title: General Consent-to-Evidence Pattern
section.t: Regardless of the specific OAuth grant type, evidence collection follows a common pattern:

ol.li: The AS receives an authorization request from a client (which may be acting on behalf of an AI agent).

The AS determines that user consent is required and presents a consent interface to the user. The consent interface displays a human-readable description of the requested operation (the displayed_content).
The user reviews the displayed content and performs a confirmation action (e.g., clicking an "Allow" button, providing biometric input, entering a PIN).
The AS captures the interaction details (what was displayed, what action the user took, when, and in what session context) and constructs the evidence object as defined in .
The AS signs the evidence record and includes it in the issued access token.

section.t: The following diagram illustrates this pattern:

figure.artwork: Client/Agent Authorization Server User | | | |-- authorization req --->| | | | | | |--- consent UI ---------->| | | (displayed_content) | | | | | |<-- user action ----------| | | (button_click, etc.) | | | | | | [capture evidence] | | | [sign with as_signature]| | | | |<-- access token --------| | | (with evidence) | | | | |

section.title: Consent UI to Evidence Field Mapping
section.t: Each field in the evidence object corresponds to a specific event during the consent interaction:

table.name: Consent UI Event to Evidence Field Mapping

tr.td: The text shown to the user describing the requested operation
How the user responded (button click, biometric, PIN, etc.)
Server-side time when the user's action was received

section.title: Example: JWT Grant Interaction Response Flow
section.t: The JWT Grant Interaction Response () defines a mechanism for AI agents to obtain user consent from an external Authorization Server. The following sequence shows how evidence is collected during this flow:

ol.li: An AI agent sends a token request to the AS using a JWT authorization grant (), including the requested scope and authorization_details.

The AS validates the agent's identity and determines that user interaction is required. It responds with an interaction_required error containing an interaction_uri (a URL hosted by the AS for the consent interface) and a polling interval.
The agent opens the interaction_uri in the user's browser. The AS presents a consent page showing the interpreted operation (e.g., "Add items under $50 to cart on your behalf").

li.t: The user reviews the displayed content and clicks "Allow". The AS captures:

ul.li: displayed_content: the operation description shown on the consent page;
user_action: button_click;
timestamp: the server time of the click.

ol.li: The AS constructs the evidence object, computes the as_signature per , and stores the evidence record.
The agent polls the token endpoint. Upon detecting that the user has completed interaction, the AS issues an access token containing the signed evidence object.

figure.artwork: AI Agent External AS User | | | |-- token request ->| | | | | |<- interaction_ | | | required | | | (interaction_ | | | uri, interval) | | | | | |-- open interaction_uri in browser ------------>| | | | | |--- consent UI ------------>| | | "Add items under $50 | | | to cart on your behalf"| | | | | |<-- user clicks [Allow] ----| | | | | | [capture evidence fields] | | | [compute as_signature] | | | | |-- poll token --->| | | endpoint | | | | | |<- access token ---| | | (with evidence) | | | | |

section.title: Applicability to Other Flows
section.t: The consent-to-evidence pattern described above applies to any OAuth flow that involves user interaction. For example:

ul.li: Authorization Code Grant: The AS presents a consent screen during the /authorize redirect. Evidence is collected when the user approves or denies the request.

CIBA (Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication): The AS delivers a consent request to the user's authentication device (e.g., push notification). Evidence captures the user's out-of-band confirmation action.

Consent-Only Flow: When the user already holds a valid session and the AS determines that only operation-specific consent is needed (not re-authentication), the AS presents a targeted consent prompt. Evidence records the scoped approval.

section.t: Flows that do not involve user interaction (e.g., Client Credentials Grant without user context) cannot produce evidence records, since there is no user confirmation to record. Such flows MAY still use the audit_trail sub-object () for semantic traceability without user confirmation evidence.

section.title: Evidence Generation
section.t: When issuing an access token with evidence, the AS MUST:

ol.li: Record the exact content displayed to the user during consent;
Capture the user's confirmation action and timestamp;
Generate a unique evidence identifier;
Sign the evidence fields (id and user_confirmation) with the AS's private key using JCS canonicalization;
Include the authorization_evidence authorization details in the access token.

section.title: Consent Revocation
section.t: This section defines the revocation half of the consent lifecycle. Evidence collection () records the grant of consent; the mechanism defined in this section records and enforces its withdrawal. The mechanism applies regardless of the OAuth grant type through which consent was obtained.

section.title: Consent Record and Evidence Artifact
section.t: Two related but distinct concepts are used in this section:

dl.dd: An Authorization Server-side entity created at the moment of consent. It captures the consent event (what was displayed, what the user did, when) and carries the lifecycle state of the consent. The consent record exists independently of any access token and is the anchor for revocation.
The signed evidence object defined in , delivered in the token response at credential issuance and consumed by Resource Servers.

section.t: Because the consent record is created at consent time, revocation is possible during the window after the user has approved an authorization but before the resulting credential has been issued.

section.title: Revocation Handle
section.t: When the AS records a consent event, it SHOULD associate a revocation handle with the consent record. The revocation handle is a URI under the AS's control through which the user can initiate revocation of that specific consent record. A non-normative example:

The handle identifier MUST contain at least 128 bits of entropy so that valid handles cannot be enumerated. The handle is a lookup key, not a credential: possession of the URI does not by itself authorize revocation ().

The AS SHOULD present the revocation handle to the user over the front channel at or shortly after the consent interaction, for example on the consent confirmation page or in a consent record view. This is the primary delivery channel and the only channel that places the revocation capability in the user's hands. The OPTIONAL revocation member defined in additionally conveys the handle in the token response; that copy reaches the client rather than the user, and MAY support client-provided consent management interfaces or agent-initiated self-revocation.

section.title: The revocation Member
section.t: The OPTIONAL revocation member of the evidence object conveys revocation information for the consent recorded by the evidence:

tr.td: The revocation handle for the consent recorded by this evidence ().
A URI where the current revocation status of the consent can be resolved, for example an entry in a token status list .

section.t: The revocation member is an extension field with respect to the signature algorithm defined in the AS Signature subsection of and therefore is not covered by the as_signature. In signed JWT access tokens its integrity is provided by the token signature.

section.title: Principal-Initiated Revocation
section.t: When the user follows a revocation handle, the AS MUST apply three validation layers before executing the revocation:

ol.li: Record lookup: the handle identifier resolves to a single consent record. The identifier locates the record but confers no authority by itself.

Principal authentication: the AS MUST authenticate the user. If the user has an active session with the AS, that session MAY be used; otherwise the AS authenticates the user through its standard authentication flow. The AS MAY require step-up authentication. The authentication method is a matter of AS policy and is not defined by this specification.
Ownership verification: the AS MUST verify that the authenticated user is the owner of the referenced consent record. If the check fails, the AS MUST reject the request.

section.t: Before executing the revocation, the AS MUST present the user with a confirmation view summarizing the consent being revoked (for example, which client was authorized, which scopes were granted, and when). Retrieving the revocation handle with HTTP GET MUST only render this confirmation view and MUST NOT perform the revocation. The revocation MUST be executed by an explicit user action (for example, an HTTP POST request) protected against cross-site request forgery.
In summary, the authorization server MUST authenticate the user before honoring a revocation request, and MUST verify that the authenticated user is the owner of the referenced consent record.

section.title: Revocation Semantics by Phase
section.t: The effect of a revocation depends on the lifecycle phase of the consent:

dl.dd: There is no consent record to revoke. The user refuses the request through the consent interface presented during the authorization flow.

The AS invalidates the pending authorization by applying the cancellation semantics defined by the host protocol. For example, in the Deferred Token Response flow , the deferral code is invalidated and subsequent polling requests return access_denied. Where issuance and revocation can race, the AS MUST evaluate the revocation state atomically with credential issuance.

The AS revokes the issued tokens as appropriate per , SHOULD reflect the revocation in a status mechanism such as a token status list , and MAY propagate the revocation event to downstream subscribers using a shared signals mechanism such as CAEP .

section.t: This specification defines the revocation trigger and the consent record state. It does not redefine the cancellation or token revocation semantics of any host protocol; those semantics are applied as defined by the respective protocol.

section.title: Consent Record Status
section.t: Upon revocation, the AS SHOULD update the consent record with:

ul.li: revoked_at: the timestamp of the revocation;

revocation_method: how the revocation was initiated. Implementations SHOULD use values from the following set: principal (the user revoked through the mechanism defined in this section), client (the client cancelled or revoked through its own channel), expired (the consent lapsed), or administrator (revoked by an operator of the AS).

section.t: These fields are maintained on the AS and are not included in access tokens. They support audit and dispute resolution, including the question of whether a contested operation occurred before or after consent was withdrawn.

section.title: Evidence Verification
section.t: Resource Servers MAY verify the evidence object by:

ol.li: Extracting the as_signature from the evidence;
Verifying the signature using the AS's public key;

section.t: Note: The displayed_content field records what was shown to the user during consent. The RS typically does not have direct knowledge of the consent interaction and therefore cannot independently verify this field. Instead, the RS relies on the AS signature as proof that the AS witnessed the user's consent to the described operation.

section.title: Audit Logging
section.t: Resource Servers SHOULD log evidence information for audit purposes, including:

ul.li: Evidence ID;
User confirmation timestamp;
Displayed content summary;
Operation performed;
Outcome (success/failure).

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: This section discusses security considerations specific to authorization evidence in OAuth 2.0. General OAuth 2.0 security considerations, including token threats and countermeasures, are described in .

section.title: Signature Verification
section.t: The AS signature over the evidence fields (id and user_confirmation) is critical for evidence integrity. Implementations MUST:

ul.li: Use strong cryptographic algorithms (e.g., RS256, ES256);
Protect AS signing keys appropriately;
Rotate keys periodically with proper key management.

section.title: Evidence Tampering and Trust in the AS
section.t: The evidence object is protected by the access token's signature. However, the as_signature field provides an additional layer of protection specifically for the user confirmation record.

It is important to understand the trust boundary of the evidence mechanism: the as_signature provides cryptographic proof that the AS recorded a user confirmation. It does not independently prove that the user actually consented. The AS controls both the consent interaction and the signing key, so a compromised or malicious AS could fabricate evidence records. Trust in the evidence record therefore depends on trust in the AS and its operational security. Deployments requiring stronger non-repudiation guarantees SHOULD supplement this mechanism with user-side signatures or independent consent auditing.

section.title: Replay Attacks
section.t: Evidence records are bound to specific access tokens. The evidence ID and timestamp help detect attempts to reuse evidence across different authorization contexts.

section.title: Token-Evidence Binding
section.t: The evidence object is embedded in a signed access token (), which provides integrity protection at the token level. The inner as_signature provides a second, independent integrity layer specifically over the user confirmation record. This dual-signature design ensures that:

ul.li: Evidence fields cannot be modified within a valid token (the inner AS signature would be invalidated);
Evidence can be independently verified even when extracted from the token (e.g., via introspection) using the as_signature.

section.t: Implementations MUST NOT copy an evidence object from one access token into another without re-validating the as_signature and confirming that the evidence id and timestamp are consistent with the new token's context.

The dual-signature design described above applies to signed JWT access tokens (). When opaque (reference) tokens are used, the evidence object is not embedded in the token itself and MUST be retrieved by the RS via token introspection () or a dedicated evidence retrieval endpoint. In this case, the as_signature provides the sole integrity protection for the evidence record, and implementations MUST ensure that the transport between the RS and the introspection or retrieval endpoint is protected with TLS.

section.title: Cross-Domain Evidence Verification
section.t: In cross-domain scenarios where the RS is in a different trust domain than the AS, the RS must be able to verify the as_signature using the AS's public key. Implementations SHOULD:

ul.li: Include a kid (Key ID) in the JWS header of the as_signature to enable key selection;
Support key caching at the RS with appropriate cache invalidation to balance performance and key freshness.

section.t: When the AS and RS belong to different administrative domains, trust establishment for the evidence signing key MAY be facilitated through a trust framework, federation agreement, or explicit key distribution mechanism.

section.title: Revocation Handle Security

ul.li: Insecure direct object reference: possession of a handle MUST NOT be sufficient to revoke the associated consent record. The AS MUST authenticate the principal and verify that the authenticated principal owns the consent record before executing any revocation ();

Cross-site request forgery: a GET request to the revocation endpoint MUST only render the confirmation interface and MUST NOT trigger revocation. Revocation MUST be executed through a POST (or equivalent non-idempotent method) protected against cross-site request forgery.

section.t: When a revocation handle is delivered through a token response (in addition to, or instead of, the front channel), clients MUST treat it as sensitive data and MUST NOT expose it in URLs, logs, or user agents beyond what is necessary to present the revocation option to the user.

section.title: Revocation Enforcement Boundary
section.t: Revocation under this specification is enforced by the AS and by downstream token revocation and status mechanisms; it is not purely cryptographic. A token issued before revocation remains cryptographically valid until it expires, is revoked via the token revocation mechanisms of the host protocol (e.g., ), or is rejected based on status information such as token status lists () or shared signals (). Deployments with short-lived tokens reduce the window during which a revoked consent is not yet enforced; deployments requiring timely propagation of revocation SHOULD combine token revocation with status lists or event-based propagation.

This specification does not require resource servers to consult consent state. Whether an RS enforces consent revocation directly, or relies on the AS to revoke the associated tokens, is a deployment decision.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Evidence records contain information about user consent interactions, including what was displayed to the user and how they responded. Implementations should consider applicable data protection requirements when storing and processing evidence records.

Consent records and revocation state () extend these considerations: the revocation timestamp and method are part of the user's consent history. Access to the revocation endpoint MUST require principal authentication so that the consent history of one user cannot be inspected by another, and retention of consent records after revocation SHOULD follow the same data protection policies that apply to the evidence records themselves.

Authorization evidence and audit trail information using the enriched response pattern, providing cryptographic proof of user consent for authorization proof and audit purposes.

section.title: Complete Example
section.t: The following shows a complete access token with authorization_details containing both authorization_evidence and rego_policy authorization details types:

This example illustrates how the authorization_evidence type complements the rego_policy type (). While the Rego policy defines what operations are permitted (the behavioral constraint contract), the authorization evidence records why those operations were authorized (the user's explicit consent). Together, they enable a Resource Server to enforce fine-grained policy while maintaining a verifiable audit trail linking each authorized action back to user intent.

The act.sub value uses the wit:// URI scheme to identify the acting agent by its workload identity, as defined in the Identity Assertion Authorization Grant (). The hash suffix provides a collision-resistant binding between the URI and the agent's attestation evidence.
